observation: RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., ICLR 2024) recursively clusters and summarises text bottom-up into a multi-level tree and retrieves across levels; coupling it with GPT-4 improved accuracy by 20 points on QuALITY vs standard retrieval.
claim: Recursive cluster-then-summarise tree construction with multi-level retrieval measurably outperforms single-granularity summarisation/retrieval for tasks requiring multi-step reasoning over long text.
mechanism: Multiple abstraction levels let a query/reader draw on whichever granularity actually matches the needed reasoning step, instead of being locked to one fixed summary.

implications.text: Riemann's L0-L3 tree architecture (build multiple abstraction levels, not one summary) is validated by a directly analogous system.

observation: Microsoft's GraphRAG builds an entity graph, runs hierarchical community detection, and generates an LLM summary per community per level, then answers queries via map-reduce over community summaries.
claim: Hierarchical map-reduce summarisation over a structured graph is a viable, production-grade pattern for building and querying multi-level abstraction trees.
mechanism: Partial answers generated per community/level and reduced upward avoids needing one model call to hold the entire source in context.

implications.text: Riemann's planned map-reduce build path for large documents is structurally validated by a comparable shipped system.

observation: Chain-of-Density (Adams et al. 2023) shows human raters (4 annotators, 500 summaries) preferred GPT-4 summaries densified ~3 passes (entity density ~0.15/token) over both sparser defaults and maximally dense ones; density beyond that point hurt readability even as coverage rose.
claim: There is a density sweet spot for generated summaries beyond which readability drops faster than information value rises, and it can be found by iterative densification with a stopping rule.
mechanism: Each densification pass adds salient entities without growing length, but each addition raises intrinsic/element-interactivity load; past a point added entities cost more attention than they deliver in understanding.

implications.text: Riemann's L1/L2 summariser should target a bounded entity-density rather than maximise compression or minimise length alone; a densification-then-stop pipeline (~2-3 passes) is a concrete implementation pattern.

observation: A single blog's claim that 'refine' summarisation strategy is more accurate than map-reduce (citing an unnamed 'RETA' benchmark) could not be independently verified by the report author.
claim: Refine (sequential running-summary) is more accurate than map-reduce for narrative/order-sensitive content.
mechanism: Refine preserves cross-chunk narrative context that parallel map-reduce discards.

implications.text: Treat choice of map-reduce vs refine per document type (narrative vs reference-shaped) as a real per-document decision to test empirically, not a settled fact to hard-code with confidence.

observation: Multiple NLP papers converge that length-controlled summarisation (hitting a fixed word budget) is technically hard: models are good at stopping at the right length but bad at choosing which content survives the budget.
claim: Fixed word-count targets per abstraction level (e.g. L0 <=25 words) risk the model dropping the wrong content to hit the budget rather than genuinely compressing.
mechanism: Length-control mechanisms (length embeddings, EOS-weighting) constrain output length as a decoding objective independent of content-selection quality, so the two can trade off against each other.

implications.text: Riemann should validate not just that a generated node hits its length target but that a faithfulness/coverage check passes too, since length-conformance and content-quality are documented to trade off against each other.

observation: A 2023 survey on query/aspect-focused summarisation notes real user information needs are often closer to broad aspects/themes than to sharp queries.
claim: Aspect-focused re-summarisation (e.g. 'show me the security-implications view') is a plausible, well-motivated future feature, but not required for a v1 canonical single-tree design.
mechanism: unknown

implications.text: Scope query/aspect-focused summarisation out of v1's canonical single tree per document; flag as a clearly-bounded v2 feature.

observation: Extractive summarisation is inherently more faithful (never paraphrases) but reads less coherently; abstractive summarisation reads better but hallucinates more, and degree of abstraction (measured by n-gram overlap with source) correlates with degree of unfaithfulness (Ladhak et al., via survey).
claim: The abstractive/extractive tradeoff is real and measurable, and n-gram overlap with source is a cheap, model-free faithfulness proxy Riemann can compute per generated node.
mechanism: Paraphrasing further from the source text gives the model more opportunity to introduce content not actually supported by the source.

implications.text: Compute an n-gram-overlap-with-source abstractiveness score per generated node as a cheap faithfulness proxy, independent of running a separate NLI/QA model.

observation: Reported hallucination rates for LLM summaries: roughly 20-45% for multi-document summarisation (up to 75% in one adversarial benchmark), and hallucinations are more likely toward the end of a summary; conversational summarisation is worse than news by ~20-30 points. The originally-reported ~28.6% single-document news figure could not be found in the cited source (arXiv 2410.13961) on fact-check and should be treated as unattributed.
claim: LLM-generated summaries hallucinate at a high, non-trivial rate; this is a first-order design constraint for any generated abstraction level, not an edge case.
mechanism: Abstractive generation is not constrained to only emit content entailed by the source, so plausible-sounding but unsupported content can be produced, especially as summaries compress/paraphrase further from source.

implications.text: Every generated node needs a faithfulness check and a UI treatment for low-confidence content (flag, retry, or fall back to extractive) rather than assuming generated summaries are reliable by default.

observation: Hierarchical/recursive summarisation pipelines are a documented failure mode for error amplification: an error introduced at a leaf/lower level propagates upward unless intermediate summaries are grounded against the original input context rather than only against the level below.
claim: Riemann's map-reduce/recursive build path is exactly the architecture documented to be vulnerable to error compounding, and each level should be built (or at least fact-checked) against original source spans, not purely against the summary below it.
mechanism: Each summarisation step is an independent lossy/noisy transformation; without re-grounding, errors compose multiplicatively as they climb the tree.
context: lab, adjacent literature applied by inference

implications.text: Build L1/L0 by passing the relevant leaf source_spans alongside the L2 gists into the reduce step, not just the L2 text; use source_span as an active grounding input at every summarisation step, not just for UI display.

observation: SummaC (Laban et al., TACL 2022) repurposes NLI models for document-level inconsistency detection via sentence-segmented aggregation, reaching 74.4% balanced accuracy on a 6-dataset benchmark, and is cheap to run (no generation, just NLI inference).
claim: SummaC-style NLI scoring is a computationally cheap, meaningful-but-imperfect per-node faithfulness signal Riemann can run at build time.
mechanism: Natural-language-inference models score whether a summary sentence is entailed by, contradicts, or is unsupported by the source, giving a graded consistency signal without generating text.

implications.text: Store a faithfulness_score per Node computed via SummaC-style NLI at build time so the frontend can eventually render a confidence indicator.

observation: QAGS (ACL 2020) generates questions from a summary, answers them against both summary and source, and scores consistency by answer agreement, with the useful property of flagging which specific tokens are unsupported.
claim: QAGS-style question-generation/answering consistency checking is a more interpretable (if older, lower-accuracy) faithfulness method than pure NLI scoring, and its per-token flagging maps well onto a 'this part isn't well-attested' UI affordance.
mechanism: Round-trip QA consistency surfaces exactly which claims in the summary are answerable from the source and which are not, which is more UI-legible than a single scalar NLI score.

implications.text: Consider QAGS-style per-token attribution as a future upgrade to the faithfulness score, specifically because its output is interpretable enough to show users which span of a gist is weakly supported.

observation: FActScore (EMNLP 2023) decomposes long-form generation into atomic facts and verifies each against a source; ChatGPT biographies scored only 58% factual by human judgment, while an automated retrieval+LLM-judge estimator achieved <2% error vs human scoring.
claim: Atomic-fact decomposition and verification is a strong, well-adopted faithfulness method, well-suited to scoring L1/L2 summary sentences individually and surfacing per-sentence confidence.
mechanism: Breaking a generated passage into independently checkable atomic facts avoids the coarseness of a single whole-summary faithfulness judgment.

implications.text: Adopt FActScore's atomic-fact decomposition as a heavier-weight faithfulness pipeline once v1's cheap n-gram/SummaC signal proves insufficient, for per-sentence confidence indicators.

observation: Practitioner and product convergence (NotebookLM's citation chips, split-pane summary|source with synchronized highlight) shows that highlighting inside the source, not just citation markers, builds more user trust in generated summaries.
claim: A NotebookLM-style clickable citation that jumps to and highlights the exact source span builds more calibrated trust than a bare citation marker.
mechanism: Seeing the actual source text a claim is grounded in lets a reader verify the claim directly rather than trusting an opaque generation process.
context: practitioner convergence + shipped product (NotebookLM), not a controlled trust study

implications.text: Wire source_span into the UI as a NotebookLM-style citation: clicking/hovering an L1 sentence highlights the corresponding L3 span, reusing the anchoring mechanism the plan already needs.

observation: Ted Nelson's stretchtext (1967-1970) proposed a reader controlling text with two throttles -- one for position, one for continuous local expansion/contraction of detail -- as a direct conceptual ancestor of a zoom dial; it never achieved mass Web adoption but persists as a research/art technique.
claim: A single continuous dial that expands/contracts detail in place is a decades-old, previously-unadopted interaction idea, not a novel invention -- historical prior art, not empirical validation.
mechanism: unknown
context: historical/conceptual prior art, not an empirical study

implications.text: Frame the zoom dial explicitly as stretchtext's direct descendant in documentation/design rationale; investigate why it never achieved mass adoption (a documented risk to understand before committing further).

observation: Telescopic Text (Joe Davis, 2007/2008) is a shipped, popular implementation of word-level nested expansion (a three-word sentence expands word-by-word into a paragraph), later spinning off into a still-used authoring tool for writing teachers.
claim: Word/span-level nested expansion in place (click to expand a specific span) is a legible and engaging alternative interaction to a single global zoom dial.
mechanism: unknown
context: anecdotal popularity, not a controlled study

implications.text: Consider click-to-expand-a-span as an alternative or companion interaction to the global dial, distinct from but compatible with FT-dial.

observation: Tiago Forte's Progressive Summarization reports self-observed layer-retention rates across many practitioners: ~50% of notes reach layer 2 (bold), ~80% of layer-2 notes reach layer 3 (highlight, ~20% of original), ~25% of layer-3 notes reach layer 4 (~5% of original).
claim: A four-layer funnel with roughly these retention ratios is a plausible real-world design prior for calibrating how much of a document survives at each abstraction level, though it is self-reported practitioner data, not a controlled study.
mechanism: unknown
population: Building a Second Brain practitioner community (self-selected note-takers), not Riemann's target population
context: practitioner method, real-world use, not controlled

implications.text: Check whether Riemann's planned compression ratios (L0 <1%, L1 ~1-2min, L2 40-80 words/section) are asking L1 to do too much compression in one jump from L2, versus the smoother Forte funnel shape; treat as an A/B hypothesis, not a hard target.

observation: Journalism's inverted pyramid and the military BLUF convention both front-load the most important conclusion so a reader who stops early still gets partial understanding, decoupling reading time from understanding achieved.
claim: An L0 gist should state the document's central claim/conclusion, front-loaded, so a reader who only reads L0 gets real (if partial) understanding rather than a topic label.
mechanism: Front-loading the conclusion means any amount of subsequent reading (even zero) still yields the highest-value content first.
context: design heuristic backed by a century of journalism/military practice, not an RCT

implications.text: Prompt the L0 gist generator to state the single most important conclusion/takeaway in <=25 words, not to categorise the topic ('this argues X' not 'this is about X').

observation: AI2's Scim/Semantic Reader (integrated into a shipped product covering 500k+ papers) highlights passages in scientific papers by rhetorical role (Goal/Method/Result) rather than generating new summary text, letting readers control highlight density/opacity.
claim: Extractive, in-place highlighting-by-role is an architecturally different, lower-hallucination-risk alternative or companion to generating new abstractive text at a given level.
mechanism: Highlighting existing source text carries zero risk of introducing unsupported content, unlike generating new summary prose.

implications.text: Offer an extractive-highlight mode as a fallback/companion to generated L2 gists, used when a generated gist's faithfulness score is low, instead of silently shipping a possibly-wrong abstractive gist.

observation: A secondary-summary-only (n=12) study comparing raw text vs structured summary (table/mind-map) vs both for query-answering found accuracy stayed high (>94%) across conditions, but showing both raw text and structured summary together sometimes took longer than the structured summary alone, attributed to cross-referencing between the two.
claim: Naively showing a summary and letting the user jump to source simultaneously may slow comprehension down rather than speed it up if the switching/cross-referencing cost isn't managed.
mechanism: Cross-referencing between two co-displayed representations imposes its own attentional switching cost that can outweigh the summary's time savings.
context: lab, small sample, secondary summary only (not primary source read)

implications.text: Manage the anchored-scroll / source-jump interaction carefully (e.g. one clear view at a time, not two panes competing for attention by default) rather than assuming split-pane summary+source is strictly additive.

observation: Brysbaert (2019), a meta-analysis of 190 studies and ~18,500 participants, found average adult silent non-fiction reading rate is 238 wpm (260 wpm fiction), with a realistic range of 175-300 wpm and declining comprehension above ~400 wpm.
claim: Riemann's L1 '1-2 minute read' time targets should be calibrated to 238 wpm, not the commonly-cited but outdated 300 wpm.
mechanism: unknown

implications.text: Set the reading-speed constant used for time estimates and length budgets to 238 wpm and cite Brysbaert 2019 in code comments.

observation: Abstract-writing guidance from multiple university writing centres converges: an effective abstract states the paper's claim/argument/thesis, not merely its topic.
claim: L0 gist prompts should explicitly instruct the model to state the document's central claim in one sentence rather than categorise its topic.
mechanism: unknown

implications.text: Same as F01-17: make the L0 prompt explicitly claim-seeking, not topic-seeking.

observation: No existing study was found that evaluates a zoomable/multi-level AI summary system end-to-end against a stated time-box promise (e.g. does the '1-minute read' actually convey what a 1-minute reader needs).
claim: Whether a given abstraction level delivers its promised understanding within its promised time is an unaddressed research gap that Riemann should treat as a first-party evaluation problem, not assume prior art has solved.
mechanism: unknown

implications.text: Build a small task-based comprehension eval harness (a few comprehension-check questions per test document, scored per level) into Riemann's own test suite rather than assuming an external benchmark exists.
